analysis.one_liner: Gives free hepatitis C cure drugs to Medicaid patients, prisoners, uninsured people, and Indian Health Service patients.
analysis.headline: The bill would spend about $9.8 billion to give free hepatitis C cures to Medicaid patients, prisoners, uninsured people, and Medicare beneficiaries, but since its June 2025 introduction it has gone no further than a Senate committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a national program to wipe out hepatitis C, a curable virus that attacks the liver. The government would sign a five-year "subscription" contract with drug makers — one fixed annual price for unlimited cure pills — so that people on Medicaid, people in prisons and jails, uninsured people, and patients of the Indian Health Service get the drugs for free. It also pays for testing, outreach, and follow-up care, and it drops Medicare copays for these drugs from 2027 through 2031.
analysis.who_benefits: People diagnosed with hepatitis C who are enrolled in Medicaid or CHIP (in states that choose to join), people in federal prisons, people in state and local prisons and jails (in systems that choose to join), uninsured people, and patients served by the Indian Health Service would all be entitled to the cure drugs with no out-of-pocket cost. Medicare beneficiaries would pay nothing for the drugs from 2027 through 2031. Community health centers, opioid treatment programs, tribal health programs, and state health departments would get grants to find and treat people.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicaid patients, prisoners, uninsured people with hep C

how_it_helps.text: Entitles people diagnosed with hepatitis C who are on Medicaid or CHIP (in participating states), in federal prisons, uninsured, or served by the Indian Health Service to receive cure drugs with no cost-sharing.

Uses a subscription model: instead of paying per pill, the government agrees to one fixed annual price for as many treatment courses as needed over five years, chosen through competitive bidding. This approach was pioneered in Louisiana and Washington state and sharply cut the price per cure.
Bars participating state Medicaid programs from imposing prior authorization — a common insurer gatekeeping step — on hepatitis C screening and treatment under the program.

Appropriates $5.5 billion to buy and distribute the drugs and $4.283 billion for public health work, including grants for screening, outreach, and treatment through state health departments, community health centers, opioid treatment programs, tribal health programs, and correctional systems.
Removes deductibles and copays for hepatitis C antivirals for Medicare beneficiaries for plan years 2027 through 2031.

Requires participating state and local correctional systems to give people the rest of their treatment course after release and refer them to ongoing care, closing a common gap where treatment started in jail is dropped at the gate.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund about $9.8 billion in FY2025 appropriations (available through 2031). Drug manufacturers would face competitive bidding that pressures their prices, but they also gain guaranteed multi-year sales and a carve-out that shields the subscription prices from Medicaid's 'best price' rules, which limits the damage to their pricing elsewhere. State Medicaid and correctional systems that opt in take on administrative work and agree to complete treatment after release.

drawbacks.text: The bill directly appropriates $5.5 billion for the drug purchase program plus $4.283 billion for public health activities for fiscal year 2025, adding roughly $9.8 billion to federal spending in a single year.

It exempts the subscription prices from Medicaid's 'best price' and average manufacturer price calculations — a concession that protects manufacturers' pricing in other government programs, which is exactly the kind of discount rule the subscription purchase would otherwise drag down.
Participation is voluntary for state Medicaid and CHIP programs and for state and local correctional systems, so whether someone can get a free cure depends heavily on which state they live in.
Eligibility is limited to citizens and a long list of specified lawful immigration statuses, leaving out undocumented people even where they are otherwise in the covered populations.

Providers, pharmacies, and dispensing sites may not use the 340B drug discount program on drugs bought through the subscription, closing a discount channel that safety-net hospitals and clinics currently use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case is strong: hepatitis C is curable with an 8-to-12-week course of pills, yet roughly 2 to 3 million Americans remain infected, and the disease is concentrated among low-income people, people who have been incarcerated, and people who use drugs — groups that list prices and insurer red tape keep out of treatment. Curing people also stops transmission and prevents liver cancer and transplants that cost far more than the cure. The roughly $9.8 billion price tag is large, and the bill's concessions to drug makers — the exemption from Medicaid best-price rules and the guaranteed multi-year market — are real costs an honest supporter should acknowledge. Still, competitive bidding under a subscription model has a track record of cutting per-cure costs dramatically, so the design channels money toward treatment rather than list prices. The main design weakness is optional state participation, which would leave the cure unevenly available.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in June 2025 and referred to the Senate health committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Cassidy (R-LA), with Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), introduced the Cure Hepatitis C Act of 2025 on June 4, 2025.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action appears in the record: no committee hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action have been scheduled since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody yet, because nothing has happened: people with hepatitis C continue to face list prices and insurer gatekeeping, while drug makers keep current pricing and remain free from having to bid for a large guaranteed contract. The bill is still alive on paper, so its fate is not sealed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — the bill is still pending

for.name: Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 4, 2025; as a physician-senator he authored the subscription purchasing design modeled on his state's hepatitis C program.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two sponsors are one Republican and one Democrat, and no votes have been held, so no partisan pattern exists yet.

industries.industry: Brand-name hepatitis C drug makers (e.g., Gilead, AbbVie)
industries.note: The bill guarantees a five-year government purchase of cure drugs for the covered populations, creating a large new revenue stream, and it exempts the subscription prices from Medicaid 'best price' rules, protecting manufacturers' pricing in other programs. Competitive bidding and the ban on stacking 340B discounts are the limits on their profit.

Providers and pharmacies may not apply 340B discounts to drugs obtained through the program, closing a discount channel these entities use; the bill pairs this with audits and data-sharing to enforce it. The restriction prevents double-discounting but removes a source of margin for safety-net providers.
Pharmacies that register for the program receive government-paid dispensing fees at customary regional rates and an advance stock of drugs, giving them paid volume without cost risk.
The bill funds purchases of point-of-care hepatitis C tests and allows up to $20 million to support development of new diagnostic tests, expanding a public market for testing products.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with the Senate HELP Committee, whose chairman is the bill's own sponsor, so a markup is structurally possible. But the record shows no hearing or scheduling nearly two months after introduction, and the bill's roughly $9.8 billion direct appropriation invites cost objections in a narrowly divided Senate. Most bills referred to committee never reach the floor; unless the committee acts on it, the likely path is that it dies at the end of the 119th Congress like similar hepatitis C elimination proposals before it.
